The daf is a frame drum of the Middle East and Central Asia, a membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.311. It traditionally has a round wooden frame fitted with small metal rings, and a head of fish skin or goatskin; metal frames and synthetic heads are also made today. When played, the left hand holds the drum and strikes the edge while the right strikes the centre; the fingers are held together and then flicked open, producing a fast, sharp sound. It is used in traditional, classical and popular music in Iran, Pakistan and elsewhere, and also in Sufi ritual and in conservative Sunni communities, by women at celebrations and by men on the battlefield.
達夫框鼓的中古波斯名「達普」與維吾爾傳統手鼓名稱相近。公元前六至五世紀貝希斯敦銘: The Middle Persian name of the daf, 'dap', is close to the name of the traditional Uyghur hand drum. Its form already appears in the Behistun inscription of the sixth to fifth centuries BCE, and in the Sasanian period (224–651) it was used at Nowruz festivals and in court music, and accompanied the Iranian classical modes. The frame drum entered medieval Europe through Islamic culture; in the fifteenth century it is found only in Sufi ritual, and in the seventeenth century it spread to Europe again through the Ottomans. In India it arrived in the Middle Ages with Persian influence, and after the middle of the twentieth century it became a common instrument in folk and film music.
達夫的音色來自擊打薄鼓膜與框內金屬環。左手持鼓並擊打邊緣，右手擊打中央，手指併攏: The daf's timbre comes from striking the thin head and the metal rings in the frame. The left hand holds the drum and strikes the edge, the right strikes the centre, and the fingers, held together and then suddenly flicked open, produce a short, sharp, fast sound; head and rings sound together, giving the rhythm a marked percussive attack. Its range is mainly the vibration of the head and the resonance of the metal rings, and the volume and timbre are controlled by the striking position, the force of the finger flick and the arrangement of the rings. Compared with other frame drums of the family, the daf, having small metal rings, adds the clash of the rings to the sound of the head.
